title: Looping over arrays
learningGoals: visit every item with a loop
start a maximum with the first item

youtube.title: C++ Loop Over an Array: Sum, Maximum and Reverse | C++ Programming EP 32
youtube.description: In this episode you will visit every item with a loop, find the biggest item and start a maximum with the first item, with Xecxec the crab. 0:00 Intro · 0:15 Looping over arrays · 1:21 Find the biggest · 2:18 Best so far · 2:57 Second program · 4:08 Recap · 4:39 Bug of the Day · 5:36 Challenge · 5:59 Next episode

thumbnail.visual: big text "LOOP + ARRAY" in tomato on butter; Xecxec next to a crab walking along a row of boxes; thin black border and drop shadow.
thumbnail.pose: Xecxec next to a crab walking along a row of boxes

scenes.animation: Tomato title card: EP sticker thuds in, title stamps with a whoosh, Xecxec scuttles in and waves; thud, whoosh, claw-click, sting
scenes.narration: Today we walk along an array. We find the biggest value, and we print the array backwards.

scenes.onScreen: "Looping over arrays": numbered lines (1. A for loop visits each index; 2. A range-based for visits each value; 3. Start the maximum with the first item) and an analogy card: a teacher checking each bench in a classroom, one by one
scenes.animation: Lines spring in one by one with a pop; the analogy card slides in from the right
scenes.narration: A for loop with an index lets you read and change items. A range-based for loop is shorter, but it gives only the values. To find the biggest item, keep a variable called best. Compare every item with it. Think of a teacher who checks every bench in a classroom, one by one. There are two ways to walk through an array. Use the index loop when you need the position, or when you must change items. Use the range-based loop when you only read the values. The second way is shorter and safer. Finding the biggest item is a classic task. The same pattern also finds the smallest, the first match, and the total.
points: A for loop visits each index
A range-based for visits each value
Start the maximum with the first item

analogy.title: Looping over arrays
analogy.body: A teacher checking each bench in a classroom, one by one

scenes.onScreen: biggest.cpp: a loop keeps the biggest value so far
scenes.animation: Code types in with key-tick; butter [HL n] highlight sweeps line by line with marker-swipe; explanation card on the right
scenes.narration: [HL 6] Best starts as the first item, seventy-two. [HL 7] The range-based for gives each value in turn. [HL 8] If the value is bigger than best, [HL 9] it becomes the new best. [TRACK best=85] Eighty-five replaces seventy-two. [TRACK best=90] Then ninety replaces eighty-five. [HL 12] The final answer is ninety. [HL 6] We start with the first item as the best so far. This is a safe start, because the array has at least one item. [HL 7] The loop visits every mark in turn. [HL 8] If the new mark beats the best, we remember it. [HL 9] The best box gets the new value. At the end, best holds the largest mark, which is ninety.

scenes.onScreen: a table of the rounds: the value and the best so far
scenes.animation: Table rows slide in one by one; the row the narrator mentions glows butter
scenes.narration: The table shows each round. Best changes in round two and in round four. In the other rounds, the value is smaller, so best stays. At the end, best holds the biggest value. Notice how best changes during the loop. It starts at seventy-two, then it grows to eighty-five, and then to ninety. It never goes down. Each step keeps the best value seen so far.

diagram.caption: a table of the rounds: the value and the best so far

scenes.onScreen: backwards.cpp: a loop counts down from the last index
scenes.animation: Second program or a twist on the first; [HL n] and [TRACK name=value] cues drive the variable tracker; output panel fills line by line with a ding per line
scenes.narration: [HL 6] The loop starts at the last index, four. [HL 6] It runs while i is zero or more. [HL 6] The step lowers i by one. [HL 7] Each round prints one item. The output is fifty-eight, ninety, sixty-four, eighty-five, seventy-two. [HL 6] To go backwards, start at the last index and count down. The test says i is at least zero, so index zero is still included. [HL 7] Each round prints one mark with a space after it. The output is the array in reverse order.

scenes.animation: Dark-blue terminal: the compile command types with key-tick, the run command types, output prints in mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Save the file as backwards dot cpp. Compile it with g plus plus. Then run the program. The program prints the marks in reverse order. Notice that the first mark prints last. The loop visits the items in the opposite order.

scenes.animation: Recap lines tick in one by one with a pop; Xecxec nods after each tick
scenes.narration: Let us recap. One. A for loop with an index can read and change items. Two. A range-based for loop gives each value. Three. Start best with the first item. Four. Count down from size minus one to go backwards. Pause the video. Say these ideas out loud, one time, slowly.
points: A for loop with an index can read and change items.
A range-based for loop gives each value.
Start best with the first item.
Count down from size minus one to go backwards.

scenes.onScreen: BUG OF THE DAY: A maximum that starts at zero
scenes.animation: Butter banner drops in with a buzzer; the program runs and the wrong output appears in tomato; the fix slides in and the output turns mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Bug of the Day. All temperatures are below zero. The program prints zero as the warmest. But zero is not in the array. Best started at zero, and no item beat it. Start best with the first item of the array. Think about the data, not only the code. If all values are below zero, no value beats a best of zero. So best never changes, and the answer is wrong. Start with the first real item, and the loop works for any data.

scenes.onScreen: I asked the array who the biggest item is. It said, I will let you compare.
scenes.animation: Full tomato screen, card flips in with a rimshot, Xecxec snaps his claw
scenes.narration: I asked the array who the biggest item is. It said, I will let you compare.

scenes.onScreen: Task card: find the smallest value
scenes.animation: Task card pops in; checklist ticks with a pop; Xecxec holds a tiny pen
scenes.narration: Your challenge: Write a loop that finds the smallest mark in an array of five marks. Hint: start the smallest at the first item, and change the comparison to less than. Write your answer in the comments.

scenes.animation: Next-episode card slides up with a whoosh; right side stays empty for end-screen elements; sign-off text types in
scenes.narration: Next time: two-dimensional arrays. Keep coding, says Xecxec!

bug.error:
Program output (it runs, but the answer is wrong):

Warmest: 0
bug.why: Every temperature is below zero, so none is bigger than the starting best of zero. Start with a real item from the array.

pun: "I asked the array who the biggest item is. It said, I will let you compare."
challenge: Write a loop that finds the smallest mark in an array of five marks. Hint: start the smallest at the first item, and change the comparison to less than.
challengeAnswer: Start small with the first item. In the loop, if an item is less than small, store it in small.
